title: Epiphany and the chalked door
hookLine: many families chalk C+M+B and the year above the door, for the magi and a blessing

lines: A CODE THAT ISN'T A CODE.
cards: Walk down certain streets in January, in Poland, Germany, Austria, or a Catholic neighborhood in Chicago, and look above the front doors.
Scrawled in chalk on the lintel: a string of letters and numbers, with little crosses between them. Something like twenty, C, M, B, twenty-six. It looks like graffiti, or a code.
It's neither. The family wrote it there, on or near one particular feast, and it stays up all year, slowly fading.

teach.b: Epiphany comes from the Greek epiphaneia, an appearing, a showing forth. It's the feast of January sixth; in some countries, including the United States, it's kept on a Sunday in early January.
It celebrates the magi, the wise men from the East who followed a star to find the child.

Matthew tells it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "And entering into the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they adored him: and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh."
For the Church, it's the moment Christ is shown to the whole world, not only to Israel, since the magi were foreigners.

teach.h: NOT THREE, NOT KINGS, IN MATTHEW.
teach.b: Notice: Matthew never says there were three, and never calls them kings. The number three probably comes from the three gifts, and the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from later tradition, not the Bible.
In Eastern churches the same day, called Theophany, focuses mostly on Jesus's baptism instead. Now the chalk. On Epiphany some Catholic families bless their homes.
Chalk is blessed, often at the parish, and someone writes over the front door the first two digits of the year, then C, M and B with crosses between, then the last two digits.
C, M, B are the initials of the three traditional names, and also of a short Latin blessing: Christus mansionem benedicat.
Christ bless this house. The little crosses are signs of the cross.
Some children go door to door dressed as the three kings, singing, chalking houses and collecting money for the poor. The chalk wears away over the year, which is part of the point.
Every January, you bless the door again.

how: On or near Epiphany some Catholic families bless their homes, chalking the year and C+M+B over the front door with blessed chalk, sometimes with a priest's visit or a short prayer said together.

games.q: you're one of the magi. after a long journey, the star stops over a house. what do you do?
o: ask to speak to the king of the town.
go in, fall down in worship, and open your treasures.
leave the gifts at the door.
games.why: "falling down they adored him: and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh."

practice: Stand in your front door, or picture it clearly, and think of everyone who comes through it, family, friends, delivery drivers, the neighbor who borrows things, and everyone who leaves through it each morning.
If you pray, trace a small cross on the frame and say the old words, Christ bless this house. If you don't, simply wish well to every person who will pass through it this year.

wordCard.voice: Epiphany. The feast of the magi, when Christ is shown to the world, celebrated with a family's chalk blessing over the door. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an appearing, a showing forth, used of a god or ruler made visible.

carryVoice: Your line: Christ bless this house. Three letters, one old blessing. One hundred forty-six days in.
